sections.heading: Let me live dependent on you
sections.text: Father, you are the one who moves first. Keep me under your hand, not trying to live as if I can stand on my own. Lead me in the path where you are at work, where your Spirit is guiding and giving life. Please keep me from drifting away from you without noticing it. Don’t let my heart grow numb to your love.
theological_themes: God is the first and sovereign source of spiritual life and motion.
The believer depends on God rather than acting as an independent spiritual agent.
The Holy Spirit leads God’s children and keeps them near to him.

scripture_references.connection: Paul teaches that human life and movement are not independent from God but sustained by him. This supports the prayer’s dependence on God as the source of life and action.
Paul identifies God’s children as those led by the Spirit. The prayer asks to remain in the path of the Spirit’s active guidance rather than drifting into estrangement.

sections.heading: You give life without making me independent
sections.text: You do not push people around like dead rocks. You make us alive. But the life you give is not meant to make me self-sufficient; it is meant to bring me gladly under you. Teach me to move because you have moved me, to obey because you have awakened me, and to stay submitted to you as the first cause of every good thing in me.
theological_themes: God’s grace makes spiritually dead people alive.
Human response to God is real, but it is enabled by God’s prior work.
True spiritual life expresses itself in willing submission to God.

scripture_references.connection: Paul says God makes the spiritually dead alive by grace and then creates them for good works. This grounds the prayer’s claim that new life produces real obedience without making the believer independent from God.
Paul holds together human obedience and God’s prior enabling work. The passage supports praying for active submission while confessing that even willingness and action come from God.

sections.heading: I am amazed by the difference grace has made
sections.text: Lord, I am stunned by the gap between what I have received and what I deserve. I think about what I was without your grace, what you have made me now in Christ, and where you are bringing me. I deserved judgment, yet you have set my face toward heaven. Why am I different from what I would have been? Only because of you. I was not more ready for Christ than anyone else. I would not have started loving you unless you had loved me first. I would not have come willingly unless you had made me willing.
theological_themes: Salvation is entirely owing to God’s grace, not human superiority.
God’s prior love awakens the believer’s love for him.
The believer recognizes both personal unworthiness and God’s mercy in Christ.

scripture_references.connection: Paul challenges any ground for boasting by asking what a person has that was not received. This directly supports the prayer’s amazement that any spiritual difference is God’s gift.
John teaches that the believer’s love for God is a response to God’s prior love. This grounds the prayer’s confession that love for God did not begin in the believer.
Jesus says no one can come to him unless the Father draws him. This supports the prayer’s acknowledgement that willingness to come to Christ is itself grace.

sections.heading: What you give to a sinner like me
sections.text: How can a crown be meant for the head of someone like me? How can such honor be given to someone so often fruitless? How can such joy be promised to a rebel you have forgiven? Your wisdom made salvation come through Christ’s purchase and through real freedom. Let hell’s door tell the truth about the wrath my sin deserves. But let heaven’s gate tell the greater truth: grace is your free gift, given through Jesus Christ.
theological_themes: The believer deserves judgment but receives eternal life as a gift of grace.
Christ’s saving work purchases redemption and freedom for sinners.
God’s plan of salvation displays wisdom, mercy, and undeserved generosity.

scripture_references.connection: Paul contrasts the wages of sin with God’s free gift of eternal life in Christ. This closely matches the prayer’s contrast between deserved judgment and gracious heaven.
Paul describes redemption and forgiveness as coming through Christ’s blood and according to the riches of God’s grace. This supports the prayer’s language of salvation as both purchase and freedom.
Paul teaches that Christ redeemed his people from the curse by bearing it himself. This illuminates the prayer’s confession that deserved wrath is answered by Christ’s saving purchase.

sections.heading: Bring me safely home
sections.text: I know sin has brought suffering into my life, and I know my own sin has never been harmless. But I also know that, in the place you are bringing me, both sin and suffering will be gone. Bring me to that safe harbor. Let this long voyage end with me home in your presence. Let the winds of your mercy carry me there and not leave me to myself.
theological_themes: Suffering is connected to the reality of sin and the fallen world.
The Christian hope includes the final end of sin, suffering, and death.
God’s mercy carries the believer safely to his eternal home.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes creation’s present bondage and groaning under futility, while believers wait for final redemption. This supports the prayer’s link between sin’s broken world and the longing for complete deliverance.
John’s vision of the new creation promises God’s dwelling with his people and the end of death, mourning, crying, and pain. This grounds the prayer’s hope that suffering will cease in God’s presence.
Peter says believers are guarded by God’s power through faith for a salvation ready to be revealed. This supports the request to be carried safely home by God’s mercy and grace.

sections.heading: Draw me closer until the end
sections.text: Let your love pull me nearer to you. Loosen sin’s grip on me. Make the world’s promises less powerful in my heart. Teach me to put to death what still belongs to my old life, and make me ready for the day I leave this life behind. Until then, keep me by your grace as I cross this stormy sea.
theological_themes: God’s love draws the believer into deeper communion with him.
Sanctification includes being weaned from sin and the world’s false attractions.
The believer needs preserving grace through life and readiness for death.

scripture_references.connection: Paul says grace trains believers to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions while waiting for Christ. This supports the prayer’s request that God’s love and grace detach the heart from sin and the world.
Paul calls believers who have been raised with Christ to seek the things above and put earthly sin to death. This grounds the prayer’s desire to be made ready for heaven by present holiness.
Jude praises God as the one able to keep his people from stumbling and present them blameless with joy. This supports the prayer’s final appeal for preserving grace until the end.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original strongly emphasizes God’s prior action in salvation and human dependence on grace. This reflects a Reformed/Puritan theological framework and may be doctrinally contested by Christians who describe human freedom and prevenient grace differently.

The original says the speaker’s sufferings are the result of sinning. Rendered carefully as sin bringing suffering into the speaker’s life and the fallen world, while retaining personal responsibility; Scripture does not support treating every particular suffering as punishment for a specific personal sin.
significant_interpretive_choices: “Supreme Moving Cause” was rendered as God being the one who moves first and the first cause of every good thing in the believer, preserving the prayer’s doctrine of divine initiative without using philosophical language that would sound unnatural today.

The image of God not moving people like stones was preserved because it is a concrete and important nuance: God’s sovereignty gives life and willing obedience rather than making people mechanical objects.
The contrast between hell deserved and heaven given was kept plainly, because it is central to the original’s moral seriousness and doctrine of grace.
The sailing and harbor imagery was retained as the prayer’s closing picture of being carried by mercy through a dangerous life into God’s presence.
